title: The Importance of 'Durability' in the Physiological Profiling of Endurance Athletes
authors: Maunder E, Seiler S, Mildenhall MJ, Kilding AE, Plews DJ
population: Endurance athletes (narrative review with field data)
findings: Physiological attributes measured in rested athletes change during prolonged exercise.
Ignoring these shifts affects intensity regulation, quantifying adaptations, training-load programming and the prediction of exercise performance.
The authors define durability as the time of onset and magnitude of deterioration in physiological-profiling characteristics during prolonged exercise, and argue that models should quantify it.
Physiological-profiling attributes measured in rested athletes are not static; they change over time during prolonged exercise.
Unaccounted shifts affect the accuracy of intensity regulation in long sessions or races, quantifying training adaptations, training-load programming and monitoring, and performance prediction.
Proposes defining durability as the time of onset and magnitude of deterioration in physiological-profiling characteristics during prolonged exercise.
Argues for profiling models that quantify each athlete's durability.
limitations: Narrative review and position argument; no prediction-accuracy figures in the abstract; author list beyond the first three taken from Crossref ordering not fully checked.
implications: Fresh-state fitness estimates (CS, VDOT) should be paired with a durability term for long races.
Durability should be a tracked athlete parameter, estimated from long-run data.
Treat fresh-state thresholds (LT, CS, HR zones) as optimistic late in long runs: store a per-athlete durability descriptor with two parts, onset (km or minutes) and magnitude of deterioration.

For long-run and ultra plans, set late-session intensity targets from a durability-adjusted threshold rather than the rested value; magnitude parameters come from the empirical papers, not this review.
